author: Payton Cavanaugh
title: 'Stop pointing fingers and start lending a hand': Albany community responds to youth violence - NewsBreak
text:
By Payton Cavanaugh ,
51 minutes ago
ALBANY, N.Y. ( NEWS10 )-- In the aftermath of multiple instances of youth violence in Albany, including the death of a 15-year-old boy this weekend, one local organization is reaching out to the communities most affected. Albany SNUG, alongside other community partners, took to the corner of Hudson Ave and Partridge Street this afternoon for what they call a shooting response gathering. NEWS10’s Payton Cavanaugh spoke with community leaders, residents, and children in the Pine Hills neighborhood to better understand what they feel is missing from the conversations surrounding youth violence.
One thing came through clearly – the kids want to feel heard. Not just after something happens, but before it does.
“What's the reason we're out here,” asked young Ahayla’s mother, Loneita McLean.
Ahayla responded while standing on the sidewalk with a sign in her hands, reading “Honk if you’re against gun violence.”
Download our WTEN+ streaming app on Roku, Fire TV and Apple TV! “To help the people who died last week,” she said, “and to make sure the people around here are safe so the same thing doesn't happen to other people.”
That sentiment echoed from local leaders, like youth advocate Eric Thompson.
“At the end of the day, we are making a vital error, by not giving these children a voice,” he noted.
In response to another shooting that left a 15-year-old dead, and a seventeen year old, and eighteen year old injured, the community showed up in numbers.
“Albany is so small, nine times out of ten, you know somebody, you know, they’re somebody’s next door neighbors, somebody's grandkids, somebody you grew up with,” explained McLean. “You have these kids that's going through something they're not voicing. Sometimes they don't want to talk. Sometimes being there is just enough."
In the midst of the gathering were conversations about exactly what could change these cycles of violence.
Get the latest news, weather, sports and entertainment delivered right to your inbox! “They want to point the finger at the kids,” stated Thompson. “Let's start pointing fingers at redlining, pointing fingers at the historical injustice that's taken place in Albany that has put people in the situations that they are in. Let’s not condemn the person because they don't have anywhere to live. Let's ask ourselves, why don't they have a place to live? Why are they in a society that seems overabundant but they feel like they have nothing to the point that they would take somebody's life and not mind that their lives are being taken."
Keadden Riggins, a local resident, shared similar concerns.
“I have dealt with this type of lifestyle since I was 13 years old, I'm currently out of it,” he said. “A lot of kids don't have a father figure or a brother figure in their life to show them the right path. They think at a young age that they join, you know, these gangs or anything else, that they have to live that type of lifestyle. But there are other parts and other ways of going about these things.”
Community members noted the importance of education, resources, and genuine understanding.
“There's no unity without community and with unity, there's the letter I,” added SNUG Site Administrator Mercedes Walkie. “So it has to take a person to be involved, the individual. And then it’s a domino effect."
SNUG Program Manager Gordon Davis explained the long-term effects instances of gun violence have on those experiencing it.
“It becomes a memory that taunts and brings bad memories to them every time they have to think about it, retraumatizes them every time they wake up, it makes them withdrawn," he stated.
As the Albany Police Department continues to investigate the circumstances surrounding the shooting this weekend, we asked community members what they want the public to know most.
“Speak up,” said Riggins. “You're telling me that there's all these people and there's not one video of the situation that happened. Put it like this. Think about if that was one of your family members.”
“You are one call away, to changing a youth's life,” noted Walkie.
In closing, Riggins and Thompson said the following.
“At the end of the day, it’s the kids that need to be listening, and we need to listen to the kids most definitely,” they said. “We’ve got to stop pointing fingers and start lending a hand.”
